title: Unanimous agreement triggers a mandatory dissenter under the Tenth Man Mandate
content:
A.1.10.2.4.7.4.7 treats consensus as a warning: "If a group of people making a decision unanimously holds a certain opinion, all make the same assumption or all come to the same conclusion, it is the responsibility of one member of the group to assume that the rest of the group is incorrect. The member of the group assigned to hold this contrarian viewpoint is referred to as the 'tenth man' and must attempt to disprove the group's decision. Where the 'tenth man' is able to provide compelling arguments against the group's conclusion, the decision must be reassessed."

The trigger is what makes this a control rather than a slogan. Unanimity itself activates the mandate — precisely the state in which a group feels least need for further examination, and the state that is indistinguishable from a shared blind spot. Note the wording covers unexamined agreement too: "all make the same assumption," not only all reach the same conclusion.

Assigning the role solves the social problem that ordinary encouragement to dissent does not. A volunteer objector pays a reputational cost and needs conviction to speak; an assigned tenth man is performing a duty, so the objection carries no implication about their real view and cannot be read as disloyalty. That is the difference between permitting dissent and manufacturing it.

The obligation is active — "must attempt to disprove" — not merely to voice doubts, and the consequence is bounded: a compelling argument forces reassessment, not reversal. The mechanism is designed to reopen a decision, not to hand a veto to whoever drew the role.
description: A.1.10.2.4.7.4.7 assigns one member the duty to assume the group is wrong and try to disprove it; a compelling counter-argument forces the decision to be reassessed.
